translations.text: Often the solitary man waits for grace, the Measurer's mercy, though he, troubled in heart, has long had to stir the ice-cold sea with his hands across the waterways and travel the paths of exile. Fate is wholly fixed!
So spoke the earth-walker, mindful of hardships, of cruel slaughters, of the fall of dear kinsmen: "Often, alone, at every dawn I have had to lament my sorrow.

There is now no one living to whom I dare speak my mind openly. I know for a truth that it is a noble custom in a man to bind fast the enclosure of his spirit and keep his treasure-chamber shut, whatever he may think.

Therefore those eager for glory often bind a sorrowful mind fast in their breast-chamber. So I, often wretched, deprived of my homeland, far from my noble kinsmen, have had to fasten my mind with fetters,
[seeking] where, far or near, I might find one who in the mead-hall would know of my people, or would comfort me in my friendlessness and entice me with joys.
He who has experienced it knows how cruel a companion sorrow is to one who has few dear protectors.
He remembers the hall-retainers and the receiving of treasure, how in his youth his gold-friend accustomed him to feasting. All joy has perished!
Then the friendless man wakes again and sees before him the dark waves, the sea-birds bathing and spreading their feathers, frost and snow falling, mingled with hail.
Therefore I cannot think why in this world my mind should not grow dark when I consider all the life of men, how they suddenly gave up the hall-floor, the proud young thanes.
A man must wait, when he makes a vow, until, bold in spirit, he knows clearly which way the thought of his heart will turn.
The wine-halls crumble; the rulers lie deprived of joy; the whole troop has fallen, proud by the wall.
"Where has the horse gone? Where has the young warrior gone? Where has the giver of treasure gone?
Now, in the track of the dear troop, there stands a wall, wondrously high, decorated with serpent shapes.
